title: Waiting for solidarity won’t work: why Africa must lead in financing its own green industrial future
body:
For years, Africa’s green industrial ambitions have been framed around external solidarity such as climate finance pledges, concessional windows, and promises of technology transfer. Yet delivery has been slow, fragmented, and often misaligned with the continent’s industrial priorities. The gap between ambition and financing reality continues to widen.

The uncomfortable truth is this: there is no automatic solidarity in financing Africa’s green industrialisation. What exists instead are interests, risk assessments, and global capital markets.

- This does not mean Africa should disengage from external finance. It means Africa must shift from waiting to leading.

Leading requires anchoring green industrial finance domestically and regionally. In practical terms, this means:

Mobilising domestic and regional capital as the foundation, not the afterthought

Deploying public development banks, pension funds, and sovereign instruments more strategically to absorb risk and crowd in private investment

Treating green industrialisation as an investment and productivity agenda, not a donor-project

Leveraging external finance to complement African priorities, not define them

- History is clear: every successful late industrialiser financed its transformation primarily through domestic effort, political commitment, and institutional innovation, while engaging global capital on its own terms. Green industrialisation will be no different.

The real question is not whether Africa deserves solidarity—it does. However, is Africa willing to assert agency, take calculated risks, and finance its industrial future with or without it?

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah African Center for Economic Transformation (ACET)
